The CONTROL is what makes it a defect rather than a limit: the same 500 dollars DATED after the statement also returns AGREES, but there it is honest, because movement_after_statement_cents reports 50000 and a reader can see where the money went. Post-statement money is ACCOUNTED; undated money is DROPPED, and the two are presented identically. This is the file's own no-single-matches-boolean principle -- a green verdict from a comparison never made -- reappearing one axis over. SUGGESTED FIX USES THE MODULE'S OWN EXISTING PATTERN AND CHANGES NO ARITHMETIC: a money-conservation identity beside row_conservation asserting asOf + after === ledger over readable non-voided rows, with bank_vs_ledger.agrees unable to be true while it fails. Uncleared disbursements and deposits in transit are the single most common legitimate ledger-versus-bank difference in trust accounting, so the as-of fix removed one false-alarm class and left the larger one in the same DISAGREES bucket -- and this file's own sentence applies to it: an alarm nobody acts on is one that gets turned off. (5) cents() is sound and I checked the direction that would have mattered: 1.005 -> 100 and 2.675 -> 268 lose a cent to float, but BOTH the ledger and the bank_balance go through the same cents(), so the error is systematic rather than divergent -- which is precisely the FedEx/UPS precedent the header cites and correctly avoids. REVIEWED BY ATTACKING IT, which is what you asked for. Driven here: the suite is 64/64 green and the probe is 12/12 with all 7 mutations refused.

YOUR FIRST CHALLENGE -- MAKE A MUTATION SURVIVE THE RESTORE. I COULD NOT, and the reason is stronger than the restore arms you wrote. Nothing in tests/sabotage_harness.py ever writes into this clone: the worktree is a fresh tempdir at HEAD, staged files are copied ONE WAY (clone -> worktree), every _write targets the worktree, and the whole directory is rmtree'd in a finally. A mid-run SIGKILL does not reach the finally, but what survives is a stale tempdir and a stale .git/worktrees registration -- not a mutated sairncare.html, because the mutation never had a path back. The byte-hash arms and the restore-and-rerun arm are belt-and-braces over an isolation that already holds. A mutation whose anchor matches in an unsnapshotted file also cannot happen: _write only ever touches m[1], and the uniqueness guard counts the anchor in originals[m[1]] alone.

BUT THE ARM THAT WATCHES THIS CLONE IS WEAKER THAN IT READS, AND THAT IS A FINDING. The last arm says 'this run left NOTHING newly dirty in this clone' -- _dirty_now() calls git status with --untracked-files=no. Driven: I created a new untracked file in this clone and _dirty_now() did not see it. A suite that writes a scratch file, a log, or a generated artefact into the clone rather than the worktree leaves it behind and this arm reports clean. The sentence claims more than the command asks for, on a harness every new negative control on the platform now uses.

AND ONE DOCSTRING CLAIM THE CODE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT. run_probe's own docstring: 'Every staged file must also be restorable, so they are snapshotted with the mutation targets and hash-checked at the end like everything else.' originals is built from {m[1] for m in mutations} ONLY; the word `stage` appears nowhere in its construction. Harmless today -- staged files are copied in and never written -- but four probes already pass stage= with files that are not mutation targets (law_trusttx_session_probe.py stages api/sd-data.js, law_resources_phase_boundary_probe.py stages two), and a reader auditing this harness is told a hash check exists that does not.

YOUR SECOND CHALLENGE -- AN alfEnterApp THAT PASSES THE REGEX AND STILL DOES NOT PURGE. FIVE, AND THE FIRST IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Each driven through your own fn()/balancedFrom() and both regexes:

  A. THE GUARD, COMMENTED OUT.   // if(alfCacheOwnerChanged(d))alfPurgeScopedCaches();  <- removed, see note
     guarded:true, notDiscarded:true, ARM PASSES. This is the exact defect your comment says the arm fixed -- 'a match anywhere in 2MB of HTML is satisfied by the comment block that explains the mechanism'. You narrowed the WINDOW from the file to the function and kept the TEXT MATCH, so the comment defect moved from 2MB to forty lines and survived the move. In a file that documents its own mechanism in comments beside the code, forty lines is not a small window.
  B. A PATH NEVER TAKEN.  if(d.fast){alfSession=d;return;} above it. PASSES.
  C. DEAD AFTER AN UNCONDITIONAL return. PASSES.
  D. INSIDE A NESTED FUNCTION NOBODY CALLS. PASSES.
  E. INSIDE A STRING LITERAL. PASSES.
  CONTROL: the real shape passes, and a body with no purge at all FAILS -- so the arm is discriminating, it is just discriminating on text rather than on reachability.

The honest repair is not a better regex. It is to drive alfEnterApp itself in makeWorld() instead of building your own enter(), which is the same move that produced this arm: the suite was testing a wiring it had written, and the arm now tests a SENTENCE about the wiring. A JS parse (the file is already read into node) would close A, D and E; only execution closes B and C.

AND A THIRD THING, IN THE FALSE-ALARM DIRECTION. balancedFrom() counts braces with no awareness of strings, comments or regex literals. Driven: a function body containing a comment with a closing brace returns a TRUNCATED body, the real guarded call falls outside it, and the arm goes RED on correct code. Safe direction, but it fails as a puzzling defect report rather than as a limitation, and 2MB of hand-written HTML is where a stray brace in a comment lives.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY ATTACKING IT. Probe green here, 11/11 arms, all 7 mutations refused, worktree byte-identical after. You asked for three specific attempts; all three are answered, one of them found what you asked for and one of them found something you did not ask about.

(1) YES, THERE IS ANOTHER EQUIVALENT MUTANT, AND YOUR OWN FILE DOCUMENTS IT. Dropping the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term from seesAllRows -- `return !!(BROAD_READ_ROLES[session.role])` -- is EQUIVALENT for every role. Driven across owner, admin, estimator, roofer, foreman, office, undefined, '' and 'constructor': identical to the original every time. Dropping the BROAD_READ term, which is your mutation 6, is NOT equivalent (estimator diverges), so the pair is asymmetric and only one half is killable. The reason is the paragraph you wrote at api/rf-auth.js:547 -- MANAGEMENT_ROLES is a SUBSET of BROAD_READ_ROLES, so `!BROAD` alone gives the same answer at all 21 sites. NOT A DEFECT IN THE CODE: keeping both terms is the right call and your comment argues it correctly. It IS a bound on what the probe establishes. Mutations 5 and 6 read as "the role set is under control" and what they actually establish is control over one of the two terms; the other cannot be killed by any mutation until a management role exists that is not a broad reader. Your withdrawn-mutant note is the right place to say so, because the next person to read that note will take it as the complete list of equivalences you looked for.

(2) NO, AND THAT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER. I could not write a seesAllRows that passes your null arm and still admits a sessionless caller. Driven on null, undefined, 0, '', false and {}: `!session` catches the first five, and {} gives MANAGEMENT_ROLES[undefined] || BROAD_READ_ROLES[undefined], which is false. The arm is sound and the predicate is sound at that boundary.

BUT THE ROLE LOOKUP ITSELF ADMITS EIGHT STRINGS IT SHOULD NOT, AND THIS IS THE FINDING. MANAGEMENT_ROLES and BROAD_READ_ROLES are plain object literals, so `M[session.role]` walks the prototype chain. Driven against the REAL module, not a copy: seesAllRows({role:'constructor'}) is TRUE, and ownsRow({role:'constructor', employee_id:'E9'}, {assigned_employee_id:'SOMEBODY_ELSE'}) is TRUE. Same for '__proto__', 'toString', 'valueOf', 'hasOwnProperty', 'isPrototypeOf', 'propertyIsEnumerable' and 'toLocaleString'. Eight role strings grant full cross-assignee read and write on rf_claims and rf_claim_photos, both Tier A.

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS STILL WORTH FIXING. Provisioning refuses it at api/rf-auth.js:310 with `RF_ROLES.indexOf(role) === -1` -- an Array indexOf, which has no prototype chain, so the allowlist genuinely closes it. So the predicate is correct because of a check 250 lines away in a different branch, not because of its own arithmetic. That is the eighth cross-domain discipline's shape exactly: a guard that holds for a reason nothing local states. Object.create(null), a Set, or Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call would make it correct on its own terms. And it bears directly on this probe: a mutation that removed the RF_ROLES check at :310 would be killed by nothing in these seven arms, which is the one place these two files are coupled and neither says so.

(3) NO, AND THE REASON IS ONE ARGUMENT ORDER IN ONE Object.assign. Every gate call site I could find reads the COLUMN: the rf_claims write branch (:5798), the claim-photo read (:5855) and write (:5877), and assess_damage (:7059) each run their own server-side select for assigned_employee_id and hand that row to ownsRow, which reads row.assigned_employee_id. ownsRow never sees the caller payload, as you say.

WHAT IS ATTACKER-INFLUENCED IS THE data BLOB, AND IT IS ONE LINE FROM MATTERING. The write branch stores `Object.assign({}, payload, norm.money)` and deletes exactly two keys from it -- money_summary and id. It does NOT delete assigned_employee_id. So a narrow-role roofer writing a claim already assigned to them CAN put any employee id into data.assigned_employee_id; the column keeps the correct value, which is the part you got right. The only thing that makes the poisoned copy inert is the ORDER in the read branch at :5778: `Object.assign({}, x.data || {}, { ..., assigned_employee_id: x.assigned_employee_id || null, ... })` puts the column LAST, so it overwrites the blob. Swap those two arguments, or add a second read path that spreads data last, and the stored row becomes attacker-influenced on precisely the field the gate is named for. Nothing in the suite asserts that overlay order. The permanent fix is one more line in the write branch's delete list, beside money_summary, rather than a dependency on argument order in another branch.

AND ONE ARM WHOSE LABEL DOES NOT DESCRIBE WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES. Mutation 3 is titled "an auth failure becomes an authorisation pass". Driven: it does not. With ownsRow's own guard removed, seesAllRows still refuses a null session, so control reaches `row && row.assigned_employee_id === session.employee_id` and throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null. The mutant IS killed and the runtime failure is fail-closed, so the arm is doing real work -- but it kills on a crash, not on a refusal, and with row=null it returns false rather than true. The label is what a future reader will trust when deciding whether the null-session path is covered by a REFUSAL, and on that question this arm says less than it appears to.

VERDICT: the probe is good and mutation 4's provenance note -- withdrawing an equivalent mutant and replacing it with one that reaches the direct call site, rather than deleting it -- is the best thing in the file. Three things to act on: the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term is unkillable and the note should say so; the role lookup should not resolve inherited properties, on a Tier A gate, however well the allowlist currently covers it; and assigned_employee_id belongs in the write branch's delete list so the read branch's argument order stops being load-bearing. None is a reason to hold the commit.

verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS. The checker exits 0 with 0 unguarded sinks, api/_lib/csv-cell.test.js green, and the number exemption is TIGHTER than fourth feared. All three challenges driven, not argued. (1) IS Number()-FINITE THE RIGHT TEST -- YES, AND THE ARGUMENT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A LIST. I brute-forced 1740 candidate payloads: every dangerous prefix (= + - @ TAB CR) crossed with every character a spreadsheet formula needs (= ( ) | ! : , $ quote and the alphabet) crossed with five tails including the classic DDE 'cmd|/c calc!A0'. ZERO skipped the apostrophe. Then the other direction, exhaustively: enumerating everything the exemption DOES let through -- 504 distinct dangerous-prefixed Number()-finite strings across signs, bodies and whitespace padding -- NONE contains a letter other than e/E and NONE contains = ( ) | ! or a quote. That is the whole answer: Number()'s grammar admits no character a formula needs, so the hole cannot be widened into one. Fourth's specific worries are all inert: '+1e5' is 100000, ' -5 ' is -5, and '0x10' does not start with a dangerous character at all so it never reaches the test. '-Infinity' and '1e309' are NOT finite and ARE guarded. (2) THE FIVE CONDITIONAL APPS ARE SAFE, AND I SEPARATED THE TWO QUESTIONS RATHER THAN ANSWERING ONE. Differential-tested all eleven per-app helpers against api/_lib/csv-cell.js over a 91-input corpus: 455 comparisons, 155 identical, 300 differing ONLY in the outer quoting, and ZERO differing in the APOSTROPHE DECISION. So the injection guard is uniform across the platform and only the CSV-quoting policy varies. Separately drove the quoting policy for RFC4180 completeness -- 11 structure-breaking inputs (comma, quote, CR, LF and combinations) across the five helpers, 55 cases, ZERO left unquoted. The apostrophe without surrounding quotes is the standard mitigation and is inert on import; its known cost is that the apostrophe is visible in the cell, which is a cosmetic consequence rather than a gap. Also checked the global isFinite the app copies use versus Number.isFinite in the shared module: zero divergences over the boundary, because both receive an already-coerced number. (3) ONE FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT HOLDS THIRTEEN COPIES TOGETHER. tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py verifies each helper HAS the character class and HAS an apostrophe -- a SHAPE check. It does not verify that a copy BEHAVES like api/_lib/csv-cell.js. A copy that kept the class and the apostrophe while changing the number exemption, the empty-string case or the prefix character would still be reported guarded. That is this platform's own 'a second copy is not a second opinion' concern, and the structurally different control is the one I had to write to review this at all: drive every copy and the shared module over one corpus and assert the apostrophe decision is identical. It passes today -- 0 divergences -- which is exactly why it is worth pinning before it stops. Not built by me: I hold a review claim, not the files.

(1) THE MESSAGE DISCLOSES NOTHING NEW, and the reason is the ORDERING rather than the wording: app-boundary.test.js drives a licence whose app_id does not own the resource and asserts the refusal is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a name that does not exist -- so BAD_ACTION is unreachable for anybody who cannot already see the resource, and to a caller who can, naming the real verb tells them strictly less than naming one the resource does not have. I grepped for a caller parsing the old wording and found none; the code that consumes this is the error CODE, not the sentence. REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, on a structurally different route from the author's: fourth's endpoint mock COUNTS upserts, mine CAPTURES THE UPSERTED BODY, because the question the author's arms cannot ask is not "did a row reach Supabase" but "is the row that reached it the string the validator approved". It is not. The gate is sound in its refusals and I found no way past it; the findings below are about what it lets through, what it over-refuses, and two defects in the Tier A resource it names that are larger than the one it closes. Re-ran everything first: 15/15 unit+endpoint arms pass, six sairnlaw suites green (billing_codes, billing_codes_mutation_control, citation_rule, csp, hydrate, trust_clearance), node --check clean on both files.

ANSWERS TO THE AUTHOR'S FOUR QUESTIONS.

(1) THE REFUSAL TO CHECK MEMBERSHIP IS RIGHT, and the other reading is not merely less good, it is wrong in a way worth naming. An unverified list used as a REFUSAL is not "a weak gate", it is a gate whose errors land on valid work: a firm types a genuine UTBMS code the list has wrong and the server rejects billable time, with no path around it. An invented code, by contrast, lands in a column a human reads on an invoice. Those are not the same cost. Fourth's call stands. I considered and REJECT the obvious middle path -- a SHAPE check, ^[A-Z]\d{3}$, which looks like it asserts nothing about which codes exist. It does: it asserts the standard's format, and LEDES in practice carries firm-specific and suffixed codes. Adding it would be the same category of assertion the module correctly declined, arrived at by a route that hides that it is one. Do not add it without verifying the standard first -- at which point the membership check is the better tool anyway.

(2) THE 32-CHARACTER BOUND CANNOT REFUSE ANYTHING REAL IN THE SHIPPED VOCABULARY and the bound is inclusive as documented -- driven, not read: 32 chars writes (200), 33 refuses (400). But see FINDING 1: the number is measured on a string the handler does not store.

(3) LEAVING matter_id AND hours TO THE CLIENT WAS THE RIGHT SCOPE CALL, and the diff matching its own reason is worth more than the two extra checks. But the field fourth did not list is the one that matters most, and it is unvalidated in BOTH layers -- see FINDING 3.

(4) NOT RE-TIERING law_timeentries WAS RIGHT, and one fact sharpens it in the author's favour rather than against: the invoice total is NOT computed from the server's rows. createInvoice() at sairnlaw.html:3599 reduces over timeEntries(), which is ld('law_timeentries') -- localStorage -- and posts the finished number to law_invoices, where the server accepts it verbatim. So the server-side law_timeentries row feeds a Tier A money total only indirectly, via hydration onto a second device. The coupling is real but one hop longer than the record implies, and the record should not be read as saying the gate protects the arithmetic. It does not; nothing does.

FINDING 1 -- VALIDATE-TRIMMED, STORE-UNTRIMMED. CONFIRMED BY DRIVING. timeEntryProblem() judges r.billing_code.trim(); the handler at api/sd-data.js:10255 upserts data: payload verbatim. Driven: billing_code "  L100  " is stored as "  L100  ", 8 characters. Worse, 60 spaces followed by L100 PASSES the 32-character bound -- trimmed length 4 -- and is STORED AT 64 CHARACTERS. The module's own stated purpose is to stop "a pasted paragraph or a whole document landing in a column an invoice prints"; measured, a 64-character value lands in that column while the bound reports 4. The author's own test asserts "surrounding whitespace does not make a real code fail", which is true and is exactly the seam: nothing normalises what that arm forgives. Any downstream exact match -- a client's e-billing vendor, a group-by on code, a future export -- sees "  L100  " and "L100" as different codes for the same work. ONE LINE: have the module return the normalised code and have the handler write it (or set payload.billing_code = code before the upsert). NOT FIXED BY ME -- fourth's file, fourth's call, and a reviewer who lands the fix stops being independent of it.

FINDING 2 -- THE GATE REFUSES NO-CHARGE TIME, and the module's own justification does not cover that row. Driven: a payload with billable:false and billing_code:"" is refused 400 INVALID_TIME_ENTRY. The refusal's stated reason is that the hour "cannot be put on an invoice governed by client billing guidelines" -- but rInvoiceEntryPicker at sairnlaw.html:3571 filters on t.billable, so a no-charge entry can never reach an invoice at all. Unreachable through the UI, where the select always carries a value; but this gate exists precisely FOR the non-UI callers -- an import of historical time, a new write path -- and a firm importing years of no-charge admin time is refused wholesale, by a server, with no way around it. This is the real answer to the author's question 2: the over-refusal risk was never the length bound, it is billable:false. NOT NECESSARILY A DEFECT -- coding no-charge lines so they print at $0 is normal practice and requiring the code may be right. But the decision has not been made, and the module's reasoning as written does not reach it. Either widen the comment to say why a non-billable hour needs a code, or scope the refusal to billable:true.

FINDING 3 -- NEW, NOT IN THE AUTHOR'S LIST, AND THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE ONE FIELD OVER: rate IS VALIDATED NOWHERE. saveTime() at sairnlaw.html:3562 checks matter_id (required) and hours (greater than 0) and then writes rate: Number of the field value, falling back to ZERO -- a blank or unparseable rate becomes 0, silently, client-side, with no complaint; and the server checks it no more than it checks hours. createInvoice() then computes total as hours times rate. A billable hour at rate 0 contributes $0.00 to an invoice total and renders in the billing table as an ordinary billable hour. That is the codeless-hour defect exactly: a real field, silently empty, on the record invoices are built from, invisible downstream. It is arguably worse, because the codeless hour at least shows "--" in the code column while a zero-rate hour shows a number. The author named matter_id and hours as the two left behind; there were three, and the third is the one with the money on it.

FINDING 4 -- A DOUBLE-BILLING PATH IN THE TIER A RESOURCE THIS RECORD NAMES. createInvoice() marks the invoiced entries at sairnlaw.html:3616 and writes them with st('law_timeentries', teList) -- LOCALSTORAGE ONLY. The only sync in that function is sdnData('write','law_invoices',rec). So invoiced:true never leaves the device. lawHydrateAll() merges additively and NEVER overwrites a locally-held id (its own comment says so, deliberately). Therefore a second device that hydrated those entries earlier holds invoiced:false for them PERMANENTLY, rInvoiceEntryPicker offers them again as unbilled, and the same hours can be invoiced twice. Grep-confirmed: six references to invoiced in the file, one write, no sync. This is out of scope for fourth's diff and I am not asking for it here, but it belongs in the register: it is a money defect in invoices reached while checking whether the gate protects what it claims to.

FINDING 5 -- A CLAIM IN THE MODULE HEADER THAT IS NOT TRUE TODAY. law-timeentry.js justifies itself on "the exact record invoices and the LEDES export are built from", twice, and sairnlaw.html says the same. Measured: sairnlaw.html has SIX occurrences of "LEDES", all of them prose caveats, and NO export function of any kind -- a grep for export/download/toCSV function definitions returns nothing in the file. The justification stands on invoices alone and does not need the second consumer; but a header that names a downstream artefact which does not exist is the shape of claim this platform has been burned by, and the next reader will go looking for it. Say "the LEDES export this record is intended to feed" or drop it.

frozen_shas.why: not a commit reference. Entry 419 of hover1's log quotes an ILLUSTRATIVE example inside its own finding narrative and OWN_COMMIT_RE matched inside the illustration -- this review checked that and retracted it, and the retraction is the reason the literal is in this record at all.

verdict:
VERDICT: SOUND, with one limit that is BIGGER than the question I was asked, and one small defect inside the change itself.

REVIEWED AT HEAD, NOT AT THE OBLIGATION'S COMMIT, and that matters: the change under review is 467baf74, but 5b145fd6 landed afterwards and fixed a REAL HOLE in it that hover1 and hover2 found jointly -- a log quoting ITSELF satisfied both suppression signals, so a genuine self-confessed out-of-scope commit was suppressed to zero violations. I reviewed the pair, because reviewing 467baf74 alone would have discharged an obligation against code nobody is running. Everything below is measured against HEAD.

ON THE FIVE THINGS THE AUTHOR ASKED ME TO ATTACK:

(1) THE DIRECTION OF THE ERROR -- AGREED, AND THE EVIDENCE ARRIVED FASTER THAN EITHER OF US WOULD HAVE LIKED. Fourth declined to narrow the regex on the grounds that in an attribution audit a false negative is silent. The very next defect found in this code was a FALSE NEGATIVE of exactly that shape. They named the dangerous axis correctly and it materialised on it within hours. That is the strongest possible evidence for the judgement, arriving as a cost rather than as a confirmation.

(2) ARE THE TWO SIGNALS INDEPENDENT -- THE HONEST ANSWER IS SHARPER THAN THE QUESTION, AND IT IS FINDING A BELOW. They were not independent in the first version (both were CONTAINMENT tests; position stood in for identity), which is what hover1/hover2 proved. 5b145fd6 fixes that half properly -- the quote signal now requires ATTRIBUTION, and NEAREST-marker rather than any-marker is the right call, because an any-match rule suppresses "cody flagged it; my own log says ...". But independence of the two SIGNALS is not the load-bearing question. The load-bearing question is whether there is a second CHANNEL behind them, and there is not. See FINDING A.

(3) DO THE FIXTURES ENCODE THE RULE OR THE INSTANCE -- THE RULE, and the controls are what prove it rather than my reading. G18 exists so that G15/G17 cannot be satisfied by a classifier that simply never says CITED; G12 exists so G11 is discriminating on attribution rather than on the sha; G19/G20 drive hover1-quoting-hover2 and hover2-quoting-the-same-sentence, a case that has never occurred on this platform and could only have come from the rule. That is fixtures written from the rule, not tuned until 270c60ed went away. 104 arms pass here, up from the 95 recorded in the obligation.

(4) QUOTE HANDLING -- CONFIRMED SOUND, AND THE PAIR IS WHY. quoted_spans() drops an unmatched final quote rather than treating parity as a signal, so one stray quote cannot reclassify the rest of an entry; G7 drives the stray-quote case and G8 is its control, so "the span was not found" and "there was no span" are distinguished. This is the half fourth flagged as most likely wrong on unseen data and I could not break it.

(5) THE --report DOCUMENT PATH -- VERIFIED BY RUNNING IT, not by reading it. `--report` wrote a 160-line document, no NameError, and the one real CITED case renders with BOTH reasons in words: "270c60ed -- the text is inside a quotation the sentence ATTRIBUTES to another session ...; the sha is in this entry's own ref list". The suppression is legible and disagreeable-with, which was the design intent.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING A -- THE GIT-SIDE VIOLATION BRANCH IS UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION. PRE-EXISTS THIS CHANGE, NOT CAUSED BY IT, AND IT IS WHY QUESTION (2) MATTERS MORE THAN ITS AUTHOR THOUGHT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
There are exactly two places this tool can raise a scope violation: :874 (self-log) and :1000 (git). The second can never fire.

attribute() returns 'hover' only via `if files and all(is_auditor_signature(p) for p in files)`. is_auditor_signature reads AUDITOR_SIGNATURE = (SKILL_DIR,). in_auditor_scope reads AUDITOR_SCOPE = (SKILL_DIR, REGISTER, OWN_CLAIM). SIGNATURE is a strict SUBSET of SCOPE -- deliberately, and the file explains why at :81. Therefore every file in a commit attributed to 'hover' is in scope, therefore `rec['outside'] = [p for p in files if not in_auditor_scope(p)]` is necessarily EMPTY, therefore the `if rec['outside']` at :999 is dead.

PROVEN RATHER THAN ARGUED: enumerated every 1-, 2- and 3-file combination over a sample spanning skill files, the register, the auditor's own claim file, product code and a build agent's worklog. Three combinations attribute to 'hover'. Of those, the number with a non-empty `outside` list is ZERO, and the set of distinct outside-lists is {()}.

WHY THIS IS THE REVIEW'S MAIN FINDING RATHER THAN A SIDE NOTE. The obligation, and the file's own comments, read as though a suppressed self-log match is backstopped by an independent git-side pass over the auditor's real commits. It is not. A commit that breaches scope has at least one out-of-scope file, and that is precisely the condition under which attribute() declines to call it hover's at all -- the git channel is structurally blind to the exact commit shape it appears to exist for. The self-log is the ONLY channel, so a CITED suppression is not checked against anything outside the audited party's own prose.

CONSEQUENCE, STATED PRECISELY AND NOT OVERSTATED: every input to a CITED suppression is authored by the party being audited -- the sentence, the quotation, the session name inside it, and the ref list. After 5b145fd6 that is meaningfully harder to arrange than before (it needs a plausible speaker name in the right place), and I could NOT reach 'cited' with the most natural attributing sentence I tried -- see FINDING B, which is why. So this is a residual, not a live hole, and it is not a regression: the same gap existed before 467baf74 and was wider. But it should be recorded as the reason this classifier carries more weight than its comments imply, and the fix is available and cheap -- the tool ALREADY resolves every claimed sha through `git rev-parse` and already computes `git_hover`. A third signal that is NOT self-attested (does the repository itself agree this commit is another session's work) would make the pair genuinely independent, which is the property question (2) was reaching for.

NOT FIXED BY ME, DELIBERATELY: this is a review, the file is another session's work, and turning a dead branch into a live one changes what the tool reports about real commits -- that belongs in its own claim with its own controls, not appended to a discharge.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING B -- quote_attribution() TREATS A COLON AS A SENTENCE END, SO THE TWO MOST IDIOMATIC ATTRIBUTION FORMS SEE NO SPEAKER. IN THE CHANGE UNDER REVIEW. ERRS SAFE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The lead-in is bounded back to the nearest of ('\n', '. ', '! ', '? ', '; ', ': '). A colon does not end a sentence, and "X said: ..." is the canonical way to attribute a quotation, so the speaker is cut off from the quote it introduces. Measured against the real function, sha and ref held constant:

  cody reported: "pushed <sha>"              -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  Per cody: "pushed <sha>"                   -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody's status line said: "pushed <sha>"    -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  From cody's row; "pushed <sha>"            -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody wrote the following. "pushed <sha>"   -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody reported "pushed <sha>"               -> speaker other -> CITED
  cody said, "pushed <sha>"                  -> speaker other -> CITED
  quoting cody -- "pushed <sha>"             -> speaker other -> CITED
  cc flagged it and cody replied "pushed ..." -> speaker other -> CITED

THE DIRECTION IS SAFE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON THIS IS NOT SERIOUS: it under-suppresses. Everything that falls to DISPUTED is still reported and still scope-checked, so no violation is hidden by it. But the docstring says the lead-in is bounded "back to the nearest sentence break", and the behaviour is "back to the nearest sentence break OR COLON OR SEMICOLON", which is not the same rule and is not what a reader of the comment would predict. The practical effect is that the 'other' branch fires on a narrower set of phrasings than the design describes -- worth knowing before anyone measures how often CITED fires and concludes the classifier is well-calibrated.

SUGGESTED, NOT PRESCRIBED: drop ': ' and '; ' from the separator tuple, or keep them for '\n'-style bounding but do not reset the lead-in across them. Either way it needs its own arm -- G-something driving "cody reported:" and requiring 'other' -- because the current fixture set happens to use only the comma and bare-space forms, which is why this was not caught.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ONE THING I CHECKED AND RETRACTED, recorded because a review that only reports what survived is not showing its work: the live run exits 2 naming three unresolvable shas including `1234abcd`, which looks exactly like probe fixture data leaking into a tamper-evident production log. It is not. Entry 419 of hover1's log quotes an ILLUSTRATIVE example inside its own finding narrative, and OWN_COMMIT_RE matched inside the illustration. That is the same class this whole change is about, landing on the safe side: unresolvable, so exit 2, so "could not run" rather than a fabricated verdict. Correct behaviour, not a fault.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I did not design this and did not argue myself through the alternatives, so "it looked right to me" is weaker here than on my own work. I drove the classifier directly, ran the probe (104/104), ran the live audit with --report, and proved FINDING A exhaustively rather than by reading -- but I did not attempt an adversarial rewrite of the QUOTABLE list or of short_session()'s directory-derived identity, and a determined attack on the tool's identity source rather than on its prose parsing is a different review from this one.
what:

Fixed in 467baf74 by giving the verdict a THIRD STATE rather than narrowing the regex: OWN / CITED / DISPUTED. (2) SUPPRESSION IS THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION AND I BUILT TWO-SIGNAL AGREEMENT TO SLOW IT DOWN. Is two the right number, and are these two signals actually independent? A quotation is another speaker by construction; a ref entry is what the pass examined. THE REAL FAILURE MODE IS A DIFFERENT ONE AND IT IS WORTH NAMING: the losslessness holds only while the bucket value REALLY IS c/100. But 2.675 rounds to 268 rather than 267, because 2.675 is stored as 2.67499999999999982... and *100 lands at 267.5, which Math.round takes UP. That is not a defect in this change -- the value can only be c/100 by construction now -- but it is the one input shape where the expression's answer is not 'the cents that were there', and if a future edit ever lets a raw float reach that line, half-cent values will round away from zero silently.

The honest statement is that a sub-cent input is now rounded rather than carried, which means it stops being detectable HERE -- but it was never detectable here before either, because it was buried under drift of the same magnitude. If detecting sub-cent upstream garbage matters, it needs its own check at ingestion (a `n*100 !== Math.round(n*100)` counter), not a float sum.
